## Purpose

This document demonstrates a complete workflow for Bayesian multilevel
analysis of sleepstudy data in R using brms, with prior specification,
posterior inference, and model diagnostics.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE)
```

## Required packages

- **tidyverse:** Tools for importing, transforming, summarising, and
  visualising data.
- **knitr:** Executes R Markdown code chunks and formats tables and
  output.
- **brms:** Specifies Bayesian regression and multilevel models using an
  R formula interface.
- **rstan:** Interfaces with Stan to compile models and sample from
  posterior distributions.
- **loo:** Estimates out-of-sample predictive performance using
  approximate leave-one-out cross-validation.
- **bayesplot:** Visualises posterior draws, sampling diagnostics, and
  posterior predictive checks.
- **lme4:** Provides the sleepstudy dataset and fits frequentist
  mixed-effects models for comparison.

```{r packages}
library(brms)
library(rstan)
library(tidyverse)
library(bayesplot)
library(loo)
library(knitr)
library(lme4)
```

## 01 The sleepstudy warm-up

> How does RT change over days of sleep deprivation, and how much do
> participants differ in their baseline RT and rate of change?

We first fit a random-intercept model to establish the workflow, then
extend it to include participant-specific slopes.

```{r data}
data("sleepstudy", package = "lme4")
glimpse(sleepstudy)

# Look at the data first: one line per person
ggplot(sleepstudy, aes(Days, Reaction, group = Subject, colour = Subject)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.9, linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Reaction time over days of sleep deprivation",
       x = "Days", y = "Reaction time (ms)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Fit a simple model first

Notes:

- We have repeated observations within participants therefore we need a
  multilevel mixed effects model.

- Given the prior assumptions and the observed data, the posterior model
  provides a probability distribution for the daily increase.

- Prior is not Truth. It is what seemed plausible before seeing this
  dataset.

- Do not mix Bayesian and frequentist interpretations. The posterior is
  a probability distribution over the parameter values, not a confidence
  interval.

- Priors can influence conclusions, especially when data are limited.

- Broadness is a design decision, justify it with domain knowledge
  Q: Does prior shows scientifically plausible dataset?

```{r define-priors}
# a collection of prior specifications
# Before updating with the observations, plausible values for the average RT
# level are distributed around 300 ms, with prior SD 100 ms.
priors_ri <- c(
  # Before seeing the data, what reaction times are plausible?
  # Around 300 ms but fairly uncertain
  prior(normal(300, 100), class = Intercept), # Set the prior for the average level
  # Before observing data, how much could reaction time change per day?
  # Usually near 0 but ±20 ms or so is plausible.
  prior(normal(0, 10), class = b, coef = Days), # Set the prior for the slope of Days
  # How much might participants differ?
  # Could be substantial, but extremely huge values are less likely.
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 50), class = sd), # Set the prior for the standard deviation of the random intercepts
  # How noisy is reaction time measurement?
  # Moderate uncertainty but not infinite uncertainty.
  prior(student_t(3, 0, 50), class = sigma)# Set the prior for the residual standard deviation
)

```


> Before letting the observed reaction time update our parameters, what
> reaction time measurements do our priors predict?

The prior predictive check uses the model structure and priors, **but
does not update the parameters using the observed reaction times**. It
therefore shows what kinds of datasets the current priors consider
plausible before learning from the data.

```{r prior-predictive-check}
m_prior_ri <- brms::brm(
  Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject),
  data = sleepstudy,
  family = gaussian(),
  prior = priors_ri,
  sample_prior = "only", # do not update the priors with the observed data
  backend = "rstan",
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = 1000,
  chains = 4,
  cores = 2,
  seed = 2026
)

pp_check(m_prior_ri, ndraws = 30) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 600)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 600, by = 100)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Prior predictive check",
    subtitle = "Observed reaction times compared with datasets generated from priors only",
    x = "Reaction time (ms)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(TRUE) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_ticks(TRUE)

```


The summary below describes the prior distributions, not estimates
updated by the observed reaction times.

``` {r prior-summary}
summary(m_prior_ri)
```
Two sets of weakly informative priors were compared using prior predictive checks. The initial priors produced simulated reaction time distributions that more plausibly overlapped the observed range and were therefore retained. Prior-only sampling implied a central baseline RT of approximately 299 ms, with between-person and residual SDs of approximately 21–22 ms; all Rhat values were 1.00 and effective sample sizes were adequate. Prior broadness was informed by domain knowledge and evaluated through prior predictive checks. To assess sensitivity to prior choice, the model will be refitted using broad, moderate, and narrower weakly informative priors, and posterior estimates will be compared.

> How much does reaction time change per day, while accounting for
> participants having different starting reaction times?

```{r random-intercept-model}
# the fitted model object
m_brms_ri <- brms::brm(
  Reaction ~ Days + (1 | Subject), # Participants have different baseline RT,
                                   # but the same underlying daily change.
  data = sleepstudy,
  family = gaussian(), # Assume normally distributed variation around each expected RT.
  prior = priors_ri,
  backend = "rstan",
  iter = 2000,   # Total iterations per chain, including warm-up
  warmup = 1000, # Sampler adaptation; learn the shape of the posterior distribution,
                 # exclude these draws from the final posterior.
  chains = 4,    # Four independent MCMC sampling chains targeting the same posterior
  cores = 2,     # Run up to two chains in parallel
  seed = 2026    # Reproducible random seed
)

summary(m_brms_ri)
plot(m_brms_ri)
# Posterior predictive check: does the model reproduce the observed data?
pp_check(m_brms_ri, ndraws = 50) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 600, by = 100),
    limits = c(0, 600)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior predictive check",
    subtitle = "Observed reaction times (y) vs. 50 replicated datasets (y_rep)",
    x = "Reaction time (ms)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(TRUE) + # bayesplot hides the y-axis numbers by default
  bayesplot::yaxis_ticks(TRUE)
```

Under this random-intercept model and the specified priors, expected
reaction time increases by about **10.41 ms/day**. The **95%** credible
interval for the daily increase is **8.81–11.98 ms/day**.

The `pp_check()` function generates a probability density plot of the
observed and replicated data. The plot shows two densities:: y: the
estimated density of your observed 180 reaction times. yrep: the
estimated density of one replicated dataset generated from the fitted
model.

The posterior predictive plot compares the observed reaction-time
density (black, y) with the densities of 50 replicated datasets
generated from the fitted model (blue, yrep). Broad agreement suggests
that the model reproduces the overall outcome distribution, but does not
establish that it captures individual trajectories.

> If I become more skeptical about large slopes, what happens?

```{r tighter-prior}
# Same priors as before, except for the Days slope
priors_tighter <- c(
  set_prior("normal(300, 100)", class = "Intercept"),
  set_prior("normal(0, 2)", class = "b", coef = "Days"), # a more concentrated prior
  set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 50)", class = "sd"),
  set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 50)", class = "sigma")
)

m_ri_tighter <- update(
  m_brms_ri,
  prior = priors_tighter,
  seed = 2026
)

# Compare the Days posterior
fixef(m_brms_ri)["Days", ]
fixef(m_ri_tighter)["Days", ]

summary(m_ri_tighter)
plot(m_ri_tighter)

pp_check(m_ri_tighter, ndraws = 50) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 600, by = 100),
    limits = c(0, 600)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Posterior predictive check",
    subtitle = "Observed reaction times (y) vs. 50 replicated datasets (y_rep)",
    x = "Reaction time (ms)",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(TRUE) + # bayesplot hides the y-axis numbers by default
  bayesplot::yaxis_ticks(TRUE)
```

Under the random-intercept model with the tighter slope prior, expected
reaction time increases by approximately **8.94 ms/day**, with a **95%**
credible interval of **7.38–10.49 ms/day**. The direction of the effect
remained consistent, but its estimated magnitude was sensitive to the
stronger zero-centred prior. The posterior moved toward the stronger
prior.

> Do participants differ not only in baseline reaction time, but also in
> how strongly sleep deprivation affects them?
